english: to submit/file (an application), to register a request
usage: Often used at a counter (창구) — you hand in paperwork and it formally enters the system.
접수 is also a noun on signs: 접수처 (reception desk), 접수 시간 (intake hours).
for the submission to be completed
The passive-feel form on confirmation screens; 접수 완료 = 'received/registered.'
민원 = a request or complaint to a public office; classic resident phrase.
examples: 신청서는 1층에서 접수해 주세요.
Please submit the application form on the first floor.
Typical instruction at a 주민센터; 접수해 주세요 is the polite request form.
오늘까지 접수해야 처리가 가능해요.
It has to be filed by today for it to be processed.
Notice the two-step pair: 접수 (intake) comes first, 처리 (processing) follows.
온라인으로 접수했는데 접수번호가 안 떠요.
I filed it online but the reference number isn't showing.
Real help-desk situation; 접수번호 = the receipt/tracking number you get.
nuance: 접수하다 (接受하다, 接 'receive' + 受 'accept') means to formally lodge something so it enters an official system — an application, complaint, or request. The tricky part is that it works BOTH ways: from your side it is 'submit/file,' but from the staff's side it means 'to receive/accept,' which is why 접수 on a sign marks the intake counter, not the act of submitting. Compare 제출하다 ('to hand in/submit a single document') and 신청하다 ('to apply/request'): 제출하다 just stresses physically turning paper in, 신청하다 stresses the request itself, while 접수하다 stresses the moment it is officially logged. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing the wrong member of the 접- family: 접수하다 (file a request) looks almost identical to 접속하다 (to log in / connect online), so learners type the wrong one constantly.

mistakes: Don't confuse 접수하다 (file/lodge a request) with 접속하다 (to log in / connect online) — same first syllable, unrelated meanings.
Saying 접수했어요 to mean 'they processed/finished it' is wrong; 접수 only means it was received and logged. Use 처리됐어요 for 'it was processed/done.'

english: to fill out/write up (a form or document)
usage: to fill out an application form
The default verb for completing any form, contract, or report.
빠짐없이 = 'leaving nothing out,' a stock phrase on form instructions.
사실대로 = 'as it really is'; common on declarations and visa forms.
to fill in according to the format
양식 = template/format; warns you to follow the prescribed layout.
examples: 이 칸은 한글로 작성해 주세요.
Please fill in this box in Korean.
칸 = a single box/field on a form; very common counter instruction.
계약서를 작성하기 전에 꼼꼼히 읽어 보세요.
Read it carefully before drawing up the contract.
-기 전에 = 'before doing'; 계약서 = contract, key for housing/jobs.
지원 동기를 어떻게 작성해야 할지 모르겠어요.
I'm not sure how to write up my reason for applying.
Real job-application worry; 지원 동기 = motivation/cover-letter section.
nuance: 작성하다 (作成하다, 作 'make' + 成 'complete') is the standard, slightly formal verb for filling out or composing a structured document — forms, contracts, reports, official emails. The sharp contrast is with 쓰다 ('to write'): 쓰다 is the broad physical act of writing anything (a love letter, a quick note, a single word), whereas 작성하다 implies there is a template, format, or official purpose you are completing. So '편지를 쓰다' (write a letter) is natural but '편지를 작성하다' sounds stiffly bureaucratic, while '보고서를 작성하다' (write up a report) is exactly right. It collocates with 신청서, 계약서, 보고서, 이력서, 양식. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 쓰다 everywhere because English 'write' covers both — at offices and work you should default to 작성하다 the moment a form or formal document is involved.

mistakes: For a quick handwritten note use 쓰다; '메모를 작성하다' sounds overly stiff for something casual.
Don't say '작성하다' for creative writing like a poem or diary — that's 쓰다. 작성하다 needs a structured/official document.

english: to be issued / to get issued (a document or card)
usage: Used for any official document you receive: 등본, 증명서, 카드, 비자.
Add 재- (再, 'again') to replace a lost card or document.
Pattern for asking how long issuance takes: 며칠 걸려요?
to get it issued by paying a fee
수수료 = handling fee; many certificates cost a small charge.
examples: 외국인등록증을 발급받으려면 어디로 가야 해요?
Where do I go to get my alien registration card issued?
-(으)려면 = 'in order to'; core task at 출입국 (immigration).
주민등록등본은 무인발급기에서도 발급받을 수 있어요.
You can also get a resident registration copy from a self-service kiosk.
무인발급기 = unmanned issuing machine, found in many public buildings.
체크카드를 잃어버려서 어제 재발급받았어요.
I lost my debit card so I got it reissued yesterday.
Shows the very common 재발급받다; 체크카드 = debit card.
nuance: 발급받다 (發給받다: 發 'issue out' + 給 'give,' plus native 받다 'to receive') is a compound that bakes the direction into the verb — it is specifically YOU receiving an officially issued document. Its mirror is 발급하다, which is what the issuing office does, so the same event is 'office가 발급하다' / 'I가 발급받다.' For residents it is everywhere: ID cards, bank cards, certificates, visas, even certificates of employment. Near-synonyms: 받다 alone just means 'receive' (too generic for officialdom), and 떼다 is a casual colloquial verb Koreans use for pulling a certificate ('등본 한 통 떼다'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 받다 and saying 발급하다 about yourself; in English 'I issued my card' is impossible anyway, and Korean is equally strict — you 발급받다.

usage: Note 으로 ('as'): you register in the capacity of a member.
등록 as a noun on signs: 등록증 (registration certificate), 등록 마감.
Common for biometric door access at offices and gyms.
차량 등록 is a real admin step for car owners and residents.
examples: 지문을 등록해야 출입할 수 있어요.
You have to register your fingerprint to enter.
-아야 …할 수 있어요 = 'only if you do, you can'; biometric access.
수강 신청은 다음 주에 등록하면 돼요.
You can register for the course next week.
-(으)면 돼요 = 'it's enough to / you just need to'; 수강 신청 = course sign-up.
새 휴대폰을 회사 시스템에 등록했어요.
I registered my new phone on the company system.
Data-into-a-system sense; 에 marks where it's registered.
nuance: 등록하다 (登錄하다, 登 'enter/ascend' + 錄 'record') literally means 'to enter onto the record/register,' which is exactly its feel: putting a person, class, device, or data point onto an official list. The key contrast is with 가입하다 ('to join a service/club/insurance'): 가입하다 is about BECOMING A MEMBER of a body, while 등록하다 is about RECORDING something into a system — and they even take different particles (보험에 가입하다 vs. 시스템에 등록하다 / 회원으로 등록하다). Also distinguish 신청하다 ('apply/request'), which is the asking step before you are actually 등록된 (registered). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'register' and 'sign up' feel interchangeable, so learners say 등록하다 for subscribing to a streaming service where Koreans would say 가입하다. If the result is a membership, prefer 가입하다; if the result is your data on a list, use 등록하다.

Watch the particle: 'register AS a member' is 회원으로 등록하다, not 회원을 등록하다.

usage: The crucial use for residents: visa, stay, contract, deadline.
Used for lease renewals and job contracts.
기간 = period/term; the most generic, safe partner noun.
Said of shops staying open later, e.g. for an event.
examples: 체류 기간을 연장하러 출입국에 가야 해요.
I have to go to immigration to extend my period of stay.
-(으)러 가다 = 'go in order to'; 체류 기간 = period of stay.
도서관 책 대출을 한 번 더 연장할 수 있어요.
You can extend the library book loan one more time.
대출 = loan/borrowing; 한 번 더 = one more time.
마감을 이틀만 연장해 주시면 안 될까요?
Could you possibly extend the deadline by just two days?
-주시면 안 될까요? = very soft, deferential workplace request.
nuance: 연장하다 (延長하다, 延 'prolong' + 長 'long') means to make an existing time span longer — a visa, contract, loan, deadline, or operating hours. The crucial near-synonym is 갱신하다 (更新하다, 'renew/update'): 연장하다 stresses simply ADDING MORE TIME to the same arrangement, whereas 갱신하다 stresses ISSUING A FRESH TERM/version (you 갱신하다 a driver's license or passport, getting a new document). For visas you'll genuinely hear both, but everyday spoken Korean leans on 연장하다. Don't confuse it with 연기하다 ('to postpone/delay'), which moves an event to a later date rather than lengthening a period — '회의를 연기하다' (delay the meeting) ≠ '회의 시간을 연장하다' (run the meeting longer). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'extend' and 'renew' blur together, and the look-alike 연락 (contact) trips people up, so pick 연장 for 'more time,' 갱신 for 'new term.'

연장하다 (lengthen a period) is not 연기하다 (postpone an event). To push a meeting to next week, use 연기하다, not 연장하다.

english: to pay (a bill/tax/fee to an institution)
usage: Formal verb for official dues: taxes, fees, insurance, fines.
납부 on bills: 납부 마감일, 미납 (unpaid/overdue), 완납 (paid in full).
to pay as per the bill
고지서 = the official payment notice/invoice you receive by mail.
기한 내(에) = 'within the term'; avoids late fees (연체료).
examples: 관리비는 매달 25일까지 납부해야 해요.
Maintenance fees must be paid by the 25th each month.
관리비 = building maintenance fee; standard for apartment dwellers.
과태료를 기한 안에 납부하면 할인돼요.
If you pay the fine within the deadline, you get a discount.
과태료 = administrative fine; early payment is often discounted.
건강보험료를 자동이체로 납부하고 있어요.
I'm paying my health insurance premium by auto-debit.
-고 있어요 = ongoing arrangement; 자동이체 = automatic transfer.
nuance: 납부하다 (納付하다, 納 'pay in/deliver' + 付 'hand over') is the formal verb for paying money OWED TO AN INSTITUTION — taxes, public utilities, insurance premiums, fines, tuition. The register is what matters: it is a one-directional payment of dues to an authority and appears on every official bill, where you will see 납부 (never 지불) printed. Contrast the everyday options: 내다 is the plain native verb ('pay/hand in,' works for dues casually — 세금을 내다 is fine and common), 결제하다 (決濟) is 'settle/pay,' especially by card at a store, and 지불하다 (支拂) is a more abstract/formal 'pay' for goods and services. So you 납부하다 your taxes but 결제하다 your coffee. The English-speaker pitfall is using 납부하다 for ordinary shopping because English 'pay' covers everything — at a shop register use 계산하다 or 결제하다; reserve 납부하다 for bills and dues to an official body.

mistakes: Don't use 납부하다 when buying things at a store — use 결제하다 or 계산하다. 납부하다 is for dues/bills to an authority.
On a bill, 미납 means 'unpaid/overdue,' not 'do not pay.' Don't read 미- as a 'please don't' instruction.

english: to process / to handle / to deal with
usage: Covers processing paperwork, requests, and getting things done.
Status word: 처리 완료 = done, 처리 결과 = the outcome.
빠르게/신속히 처리하다 reassures someone you'll act fast.
환불 처리 is a stock customer-service phrase.
examples: 신청서가 접수되면 3일 안에 처리됩니다.
Once the application is received, it is processed within 3 days.
Passive 처리되다 in official notices; pairs with 접수되다.
이 문제는 제가 처리할게요.
I'll handle this issue.
-(으)ㄹ게요 = speaker's promise; reassuring at work.
고객 불만이 들어오면 바로 처리해야 해요.
When a customer complaint comes in, you have to deal with it immediately.
불만 = complaint; -아야 해요 = obligation.
nuance: 처리하다 (處理하다, 處 'manage/place' + 理 'put in order') is a workhorse meaning to process, handle, or take care of a task, request, or problem, and the passive 처리되다 ('be processed') saturates official status messages. The register is neutral-professional, ideal for office work and paperwork. Watch three near-neighbors: 해결하다 ('to solve/resolve') implies fully fixing a problem so it's gone, whereas 처리하다 can just mean 'deal with / move it along the pipeline' without a happy ending; 다루다 means 'to handle/treat' in the sense of how you manage a topic or object; and bare 하다 ('do') cannot stand in for 'take care of a matter.' The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that bare-하다 trap: 'I'll do this issue' translated literally as '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong — you must say 처리할게요. Reach for 처리하다 whenever English would say 'handle,' 'take care of,' or 'process.'

處理하다: 處 'manage/place' + 理 'put in order.'

mistakes: Learners overuse 하다 alone; '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong. Use 처리하다 to mean 'handle/take care of' a matter.
처리하다 (deal with/move along) isn't always 해결하다 (fully solve). If the issue is actually resolved, say 해결됐어요, not just 처리됐어요.

usage: Formal 'ask' for businesses, offices, customer service.
문의 as a noun: 문의처 (contact for inquiries), 문의 전화 (inquiry line).
The place you ask takes 에/에게: 고객센터에 문의하다.
전화로/이메일로 문의하다 names the channel you use.
examples: 자세한 사항은 고객센터로 문의해 주세요.
For details, please inquire with the customer center.
-(으)로 here = 'to' that contact point; standard closing line.
비자 관련해서 출입국에 문의했어요.
I inquired with immigration about visa matters.
~ 관련해서 = 'regarding ~'; very relevant resident situation.
혹시 환불 가능한지 문의드리고 싶은데요.
I'd like to inquire whether a refund is possible.
문의드리다 = humble form to a business; -ㄴ데요 softens the request.
nuance: 문의하다 (問議하다, 問 'ask' + 議 'discuss/consult') is the formal, polite verb for making an inquiry to a business or institution — by phone, email, or in person — and it appears on every company's contact page. The sharp contrast is with 물어보다 ('to ask'), the everyday native verb you use with friends, classmates, or a stranger on the street; 물어보다 between you and a company sounds too casual, while 문의하다 between two friends sounds absurdly stiff, like saying 'I should like to make an inquiry' to your roommate. For extra deference to a business, the humble 문의드리다 ('I inquire (to you)') is common. Note the particle: the place you ask takes 에/에게/(으)로, not 을/를 (고객센터에 문의하다, not 고객센터를 문의하다). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'ask' is one word for every register, so learners either over-formalize among friends or under-formalize toward institutions; match 문의하다 to organizations and 물어보다 to people.

English 'ask' is one word for every register, so learners either over-formalize among friends or under-formalize toward institutions; match 문의하다 to organizations and 물어보다 to people.

mistakes: Use 물어보다 for asking a friend a question; 문의하다 is for organizations/services and sounds too formal between individuals.
Particle error: it's 고객센터에 문의하다 (inquire WITH the center), not 고객센터를 문의하다. The asked party takes 에/에게, not 을/를.

english: to report / to declare / to notify (officially)
usage: Required after moving — registering your new address at the 주민센터.
For lost cards/phones/passports; also 도난 신고 (theft report).
경찰에/112에 신고하다; the authority takes 에.
세금 신고 = tax filing/declaration to the tax office.
examples: 이사하면 14일 안에 전입신고를 해야 해요.
After moving you must file a move-in report within 14 days.
전입신고 = move-in registration; a legal requirement for residents.
카드를 잃어버려서 바로 분실 신고했어요.
I lost my card so I reported it lost right away.
바로 = right away; urgent, practical action.
옆집에서 너무 시끄러워서 경찰에 신고할 뻔했어요.
It was so loud next door I almost reported it to the police.
-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 = 'almost did'; everyday spoken nuance.
nuance: 신고하다 (申告하다, 申 'state/declare' + 告 'tell/announce') means to officially report or declare something TO AN AUTHORITY — a move (전입신고), a loss, an emergency, taxes (세금 신고), or wrongdoing — and it always points toward a government office or official channel (the authority takes 에). Three contrasts matter. 신청하다 ('apply/request') is the big look-alike trap: 신고 = NOTIFY/DECLARE a fact, 신청 = REQUEST/apply for something you want — you 전입신고 (declare your move) but 비자를 신청 (apply for a visa). 알리다 ('to inform/let know') is the general, non-official verb (친구에게 알리다, tell a friend). 고발하다/고소하다 are heavier legal terms (accuse/press charges) beyond ordinary reporting. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'report' is broad and friendly, so learners use 신고하다 to mean 'tell/report to my boss' — but to an individual that should be 보고하다 (report up a hierarchy) or 알리다, while 신고하다 is reserved for officialdom.

usage: The signed surface takes 에: 서류에/계약서에 서명하다.
The exact phrase staff say when handing you a pen.
to sign in one's own hand
자필 = handwritten; sometimes required over a typed name.
Said when someone needs YOUR or another party's signature.
examples: 내용을 확인하고 여기에 서명해 주세요.
Please check the contents and sign here.
-고 = 'and then'; the surface 여기 takes 에.
계약서에 서명하기 전에 다시 한번 읽어 봤어요.
I read the contract once more before signing it.
-기 전에 = before; smart habit for housing/job contracts.
전자 서명도 법적으로 인정되나요?
Is an electronic signature also legally recognized?
전자 서명 = e-signature; 인정되다 = be recognized/accepted.
nuance: 서명하다 (署名하다, 署 'sign/inscribe' + 名 'name') means to write your name on a document as a signature, and the surface you sign takes 에 (계약서에 서명하다). Two contrasts are essential. First, register: 사인하다 is a casual loanword (from English 'sign') that Koreans say constantly in speech — '여기 사인해 주세요' — but on formal/legal documents the proper written term is 서명; treat 서명하다 as the dignified twin of 사인하다. Second, and uniquely Korean: signing is not the only option, because Korea traditionally validates documents with a personal stamp called 도장, and the officially registered version is the 인감(도장). So a counter clerk may ask for either a 서명 or a 도장, and certain legal papers still prefer the stamp. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle plus assuming a signature is always enough: say 계약서에 서명하다 (not 계약서를 서명하다), and be ready to be asked for a 도장 instead.

usage: The standard office/admin verb for printing files.
to print in black and white
컬러로 출력하다 = print in color; common copy-shop request.
양면 = both sides; 단면 = single side.
Takes a digital source: 파일을/문서를 출력하다.
examples: 등본을 출력해서 가져오세요.
Print out the registration copy and bring it.
-아서 = do and then; 등본 = certified copy, a frequent admin request.
편의점에서도 서류를 출력할 수 있어요.
You can print documents at convenience stores too.
도 = 'too/even'; Korean convenience stores have self-print kiosks.
파일을 PDF로 저장한 다음에 출력했어요.
I saved the file as PDF and then printed it.
-(으)ㄴ 다음에 = 'after doing'; everyday office workflow.
nuance: 출력하다 (出力하다, 出 'come out' + 力 'force/power') literally means 'output,' and in computing it broadly opposes 입력하다 (入力, 'input/type in'). In daily admin and office life, however, it almost always means specifically 'to print out' from a computer, and that is how you'll see it on kiosks and printer menus. The register contrast is with 프린트하다, the casual English-loan equivalent people say in conversation ('이거 프린트해 줘'); 출력하다 is the cleaner, more formal/technical choice for instructions and signage. Don't confuse it with 복사하다 ('to photocopy/copy'), which duplicates an existing physical page rather than rendering a digital file. The English-speaker pitfall is the in/out pair: 출력 (out) and 입력 (in) share the 력 base and look similar, so beginners mix up 'print/output' with 'type/input' — anchor it with 출 = 'exit/out,' the same 출 as in 출구 (exit).

english: to sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan)
usage: Takes 에: you join 'into' a service or plan.
회원 가입 is the 'Sign Up' button everywhere online.
to sign up for a phone plan
요금제 = rate plan; a first-week task for new residents.
가입 조건/자격 = who is allowed to join.
examples: 휴대폰 요금제에 새로 가입했어요.
I just signed up for a new phone plan.
에 marks what you join; 새로 = newly/just.
이 앱은 가입하지 않아도 쓸 수 있어요?
Can I use this app without signing up?
-지 않아도 = 'even without doing'; avoids making an account.
건강보험에 가입하려면 어떤 서류가 필요해요?
What documents do I need to enroll in health insurance?
-(으)려면 = 'in order to'; 건강보험 = national health insurance.
nuance: 가입하다 (加入하다, 加 'add' + 入 'enter') literally means 'to add oneself in / enter into,' i.e. to BECOME A MEMBER OR SUBSCRIBER of a service, plan, club, or insurance — and it firmly takes the particle 에 (보험에 가입하다, the thing you enter into). The contrasts within this admin set are the crux. 등록하다 ('register/record data') puts information onto a list (지문을 등록하다), whereas 가입하다 makes you a member of a body; 신청하다 ('apply/request') is merely the asking step, which may precede actually being 가입된 (enrolled). 회원 가입 is the universal 'Sign Up' on Korean apps and sites. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: because English says 'join the gym / join insurance' with a direct object, learners produce 보험을 가입하다, but Korean requires 에 — what you join takes 에, not 을/를. Anchor it as '들어가다(enter) INTO 에.'
